editorNote: This issue follows the chronological 1982 series into the week beginning September 20, with Mattel's Atari-compatible M-Network cartridges, coin-op chart powerhouses, and early fall computer magazines sharing the same retail counter.
morningLine: M-Network turns Atari VCS tank combat into the week's shelf story while Abracadabra returns to No. 1 and E.T. keeps leading the box office week.

lead.headline: M-Network Tanks Roll Onto Atari Shelves
lead.summary: Armor Ambush, Mattel's Atari VCS adaptation of the Intellivision tank game Armor Battle, gives the blue-label M-Network line a clear September talking point: rival console makers are no longer just fighting with hardware, they are fighting for cartridge slots on Atari's own wall. For buyers, it made a familiar Combat-style duel look newly branded, with mines, changing battlefields, and the novelty of Mattel software running on the VCS.
lead.confidence: Armor Ambush is dated to September 1982 in Atari VCS release references; used as exact-month shelf context for this weekly issue

computerItems.headline: Armor Ambush Carries Intellivision DNA to the VCS
computerItems.summary: The M-Network cartridge translates Mattel's tank-battle idea for Atari players, extending the VCS beyond Atari-published games and making third-party identity visible on the pegboard.
computerItems.confidence: September 1982 Atari VCS release and M-Network context

computerItems.label: Arcade Route
computerItems.headline: Donkey Kong, Ms. Pac-Man, Zaxxon, and Defender Still Drive Quarters
computerItems.summary: Period arcade charts for 1982 show the route dominated by familiar names, with Nintendo, Midway, Sega, Williams, Atari, and Namco titles defining what home-cartridge makers were chasing.

computerItems.label: Computer Store
computerItems.headline: Compute! Keeps Multi-Machine Programming in Print
computerItems.summary: The September Compute! issue covers Atari GTIA graphics, VIC-20 joystick work, Commodore 64 sprites and sound, Color Computer graphics, and Apple Turtle PILOT, showing how one magazine served several incompatible home machines.

computerItems.label: Apple Desk
computerItems.headline: Apple II Sales Reporting Gets Quieter
computerItems.summary: Apple II history notes that in September 1982 Apple stopped publicly announcing annual system sales, a small sign that the personal-computer business was maturing beyond hobbyist bragging rights.

market.headline: Third-Party Console Software Becomes the Main Event
market.summary: Armor Ambush shows the 1982 VCS aisle turning into a publisher contest. Hardware makers, arcade licensors, and independent labels all wanted the same Atari customers, and the shelf was beginning to look crowded before the holiday rush.
